Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette:
Kwame, a 68-year-old policy analyst who had spent decades shaping public health regulations, never expected to become a case study in the very system he helped design. Eighteen months ago, during a routine morning meeting, a crushing pressure spread across his chest. He dismissed it as indigestion until he collapsed in the corridor. The heart attack—and the subsequent emergency surgery, the days of beeping monitors, the clinical voices discussing his odds—had rewired something fundamental. What frightened him most now was that the memory did not stay in the past. When it returned, often without warning, it felt as if he were still on that cold hospital gurney, the ceiling tiles swimming overhead, the defibrillator paddles charging. The sensation was so vivid that his body would brace itself, muscles taut, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing, overwhelmed by a flood of helplessness. He had come to believe that his own body had become an enemy, that it was no longer something he could trust. Even lying in bed at night, his heart would pound at the slightest creak of the house, and he would find himself scanning the shadows of his bedroom as if danger lurked in the corners. This constant alertness, the feeling of being on guard inside his own home, only made the intrusive memories more frequent—as if the hypervigilance itself pried the door open for the past to rush through.

The connection between his vigilance and his dark appraisals tightened into a loop he could not escape. Every time his chest tightened from stress or a skipped heartbeat, Kwame interpreted it as proof that his body was fundamentally unreliable, a ticking bomb. That belief, in turn, kept his nervous system locked in a state of readiness; he carried tension in his shoulders all day, struggled to concentrate on the policy reports that had once anchored his professional identity. He had taken to working from home, but the silence of his apartment only amplified the internal alarms. His colleagues—younger, healthier—expressed sympathetic concern, but he read pity in their eyes and withdrew further. At home, he avoided the treadmill he had once used daily, certain that exertion would trigger another event. The isolation fed his certainty that he would never feel normal emotions again; numbness descended like a thick fog, and sometimes he could recall the heart attack without any feeling at all, as if it had happened to a stranger. Yet those dead moments were deceptive—another trigger, a sudden recollection of his late wife’s face (she had died of cancer five years earlier), any mention of hospitals on the news, could collapse him back into the raw, present-tense terror.

Last month, during a virtual briefing on healthcare disparities, a colleague offhandedly mentioned the defibrillator protocol in an emergency room. Kwame’s vision tunneled; he ended the call midsentence and sat shaking at his desk, unable to breathe or speak until the wave passed. It was the first time he had to physically leave a work situation, and the shame—another layer of evidence that his body was a traitor—finally drove him to schedule an appointment. He is not sure what he wants: perhaps just to stop being afraid of himself, to find a way back to the analytical clarity he once took for granted. But what he fears most is that the part of him that can feel anything at all has been buried so deep it will never surface again.
